objective: Amount text with misplaced commas is accepted and read as a wrong amount: `1,2,3` is read as 123.00, `12,34` as 1234.00 and the European-style `3,50` as 350.00, where the writer most likely meant 3.50. A comma may only be a thousands separator. The rules: commas may appear only in the whole-number part (never after the decimal point); when an amount has commas, the digits before the first comma are 1 to 3 digits and every group after a comma is exactly 3 digits; commas stay optional, so `1234` and `1,234` are both valid. A leading minus sign, a leading `$`, surrounding whitespace and the one or two decimal digits behave as before. Amount text that breaks these rules is refused with a `ParseError`, in files as well as when parsed directly.
acceptance: A comma after the decimal point is always refused: `1.2,3`, `1.,50`, `1,234.5,0`, `0.5,`, `12.3,4`
In an order file the unit price follows the same rule: a quoted `1,250.00` is read as 125000 cents, while quoted `1,2,3`, `12,50`, `3,50` and `1,23.00` make reading the file fail with a `ParseError`

`stockroom sales --orders F` on an order file with the quoted unit price `3,50` returns exit code 1, writes `stockroom: error: ...` to stderr and nothing to stdout; with the quoted unit price `1,350.00` it returns 0 and prints `Revenue: $1,350.00`
